readerTitle: When great numbers hide a toxic culture
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Wells Fargo 판매 관행 스캔들) + 실제 연구 (Sull, Sull & Zweig 2022) + 가상 적용 (IT 컨설팅사, 레스토랑 주방)
insight: 조직 문화가 해로운지는 벽에 걸린 가치가 아니라, 무엇을 눈감아 주는지와 나쁜 소식을 가져온 사람에게 무슨 일이 생기는지로 드러난다.
misconception: 실적이 좋고 가치 선언이 훌륭하면 문화도 건강하다. 해로운 문화는 소리 지르는 상사가 있는 곳에서만 생긴다.

sources.text: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2016). CFPB Fines Wells Fargo $100 Million for Widespread Illegal Practice of Secretly Opening Unauthorized Accounts.
Independent Directors of the Board of Wells Fargo & Company (April 2017). Sales Practices Investigation Report.
U.S. Department of Justice (2020). Wells Fargo Agrees to Pay $3 Billion to Resolve Criminal and Civil Investigations into Sales Practices.
Sull, D., Sull, C. & Zweig, B. (2022). Toxic Culture Is Driving the Great Resignation. MIT Sloan Management Review.

factChecks.note: "최대 350만 개" 계좌는 2017년 8월 Wells Fargo가 확대 발표한 추정치입니다(2016년 최초 발표는 약 210만 개). 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.
2016년 벌금 $185M = CFPB $100M + OCC $35M + LA 시 검찰 $50M. 약 5,300명 해고는 2011~2016년 기간 기준으로 회사가 밝힌 숫자입니다. CEO John Stumpf는 2016년 10월 사임했습니다.
"Eight is great" 구호와 가구당 8개 상품 목표는 당시 보도와 2017년 이사회 보고서에 나옵니다. 2020년 $30억 합의는 DOJ·SEC 발표 기준입니다.
Sull 외(2022): 해로운 문화가 보상보다 이직을 약 10.4배 더 강하게 예측했다는 결과와 'Toxic Five'(disrespectful, noninclusive, unethical, cutthroat, abusive)를 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 "about 10 times"로 적었습니다.

cards.title: When great numbers hide a toxic culture
body: For years, investors praised Wells Fargo for one number: how many products each customer held. The internal goal was eight, summed up in a slogan: *"Eight is great."*
Behind the number, employees were opening accounts customers never asked for. A later review estimated up to 3.5 million of them.

image.label: A rising chart casting a dark, tangled shadow
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 반짝이는 상승 막대그래프가 서 있고, 뒤쪽 벽에 비친 그림자는 엉킨 실타래와 움츠린 작은 사람들 모양. 실제 은행 로고, 마차 마크, 브랜드 색 사용 금지.

cards.title: Your star never reports a problem.
body: You run a 60-person IT consulting firm. Your top account lead brings in a third of revenue. In two years, five people have left his team.
In project reviews, his projects are always "on track." What do you do?

options.text: Leave it. His results are great, and consulting isn't for everyone
options.feedback: You protect revenue today, but you also teach everyone that results excuse anything. Problems you can't see tend to surface late and expensive.

options.text: Give him his bonus, plus a quiet word about being easier on people
options.feedback: It signals you noticed, but the reward still says the method is fine. And you still don't know what's really happening on his projects.

options.text: Look at how he gets results: talk to people who left and check his projects yourself
options.feedback: It costs time and may be awkward with your top earner. But "always on track" plus steady exits is a pattern worth checking before it breaks.

cards.title: The bill for the numbers came due.
body: In 2016, regulators fined Wells Fargo $185 million. The bank said it had fired about 5,300 employees over five years for improper sales. The CEO resigned that year.

A 2017 board investigation pointed at the **sales culture**: targets many staff saw as impossible, managers who pushed hard to hit them, and a habit of treating each case as one bad employee rather than a signal.
In 2020, the bank agreed to pay $3 billion to settle criminal and civil investigations.

cards.title: Signs of a toxic culture
body: A **toxic culture** is one where the behavior that gets rewarded or tolerated harms people, inside or outside the company, and people learn it isn't safe to say so.

The signs rarely show in the values on the wall. Wells Fargo's stated values put customers first. The signs show in what actually happens: who gets promoted, what gets excused, and what happens to the person who brings bad news.

image.label: A values poster on a wall, with a different scene behind it
image.brief: 사무실 벽에 "Customers first"라고 적힌 깔끔한 포스터. 포스터 옆 유리창 너머로는 고개 숙이고 입을 다문 직원들, 한쪽에 박수받는 한 사람. 말과 실제의 차이가 보이도록. 실제 기업 로고 금지.

cards.title: Look for patterns, not slogans.
list: **Results excuse behavior:** top performers get a pass others wouldn't
**Bad news stays hidden:** everything is "on track" until it breaks
**Different rules by rank:** leaders skip what they demand of others
**Fear of mistakes:** people cover up instead of asking for help
**Quiet exits:** good people leave, always for "a better offer"
cards.callout: One sign is a question. Several together are a pattern.
cards.softwareNote: In software teams, look at incident reviews. If they hunt for someone to blame, engineers stop reporting near-misses, and small bugs grow into outages.

cards.title: People leave cultures more than salaries.
body: In 2022, researchers Donald Sull, Charles Sull and Ben Zweig analyzed millions of employee records and reviews. A toxic culture predicted people quitting about **10 times more strongly** than pay did.
They named five common elements: disrespectful, noninclusive, unethical, cutthroat and abusive. Each one tends to show up in daily behavior long before it shows up in a scandal.

cards.title: Hard is not the same as toxic.
body: High standards, blunt feedback and busy seasons can feel uncomfortable without being toxic. The test is whether people can still disagree, admit mistakes and be treated fairly.
Also, one bad week or one complaint isn't a culture. Look for repeated patterns. And remember that exit numbers are a late signal: by the time people leave, the damage has been building for a while.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant kitchen.
body: Your head chef is brilliant, and reviewers love the food. Line cooks say he shouts, and last month a cook hid a cut hand to avoid his anger.
Your sous-chef says, "Leave it. That's how kitchens are." What do you do?

options.text: Agree. Kitchens are high pressure, and the food speaks for itself
options.feedback: You keep the peace with your star, but a hidden injury is a safety risk. It also tells every cook that fear matters more than reporting.

options.text: Talk to the chef, set a clear rule that injuries get reported without blame, and check with the cooks in a month
options.feedback: It takes a hard conversation and follow-up. But it changes what gets tolerated, which is where the culture actually lives.
It sends a strong signal, but acting on one story without hearing him can feel unfair. And if you don't fix what let it happen, the pattern may return.

cards.title: Judge a culture by what it tolerates, not what it says.
body: Strong numbers and good values on paper can hide a culture that harms people. The signs live in what gets excused and what happens to bad news.
**Try it today:** recall the last piece of bad news someone brought you. What happened to them next?
